How to Use This Tool (More info and contact)

Refer to this Youtube playlist for a series of tutorials helping you get started.

Reference Selection:

Select your start or end book, chapter, and verse from "Start Ref" and "End Ref".

You may manually adjust how many verses to show at a time by changing the number in between "Show" and "verses" when "Fixed" is enabled.

When "Fixed" is unchecked, you select the start and end references manually.

The 'Load' button will load the current reference selection. This is only necessary when the user has searched and wants to go back to the current selection.

The "Random Reference" button will send a random verse block to the active panel.

You can save the current reference selection to be persistant using the "Lock Reference" button. This only overrides the random generation on page load.

Settings

The settings in the "Display" popup allow you to customize your user experience. The search settings will be discussed in the "Searching" section.

The options within the 'Show on Screen' box are a list of word properties that can be shown on screen. Any properties left unchecked will be shown in a popup window for each word. The options are:

  • Greek: shows the Greek text.
  • English: shows the English translation.
  • Morphology: shows grammatical parsing information in abbreviated form. Expanded grammar information is shown in the popup.
  • Strong's: shows Strong's Concordance numbers.
  • Roots: shows my personal categorization of related words by showing the etymological breakdown of primitive roots from which they are constructed. Greek has many compound words. This is meant to be a more comprehesive set of connections than the Strong's concordance numbers. However, please be careful since some of the connections are a bit more spurious than others and you need to watch out for the etymological fallacy.

Other display settings:

  • Show verse numbers: for an 'authentic' reading experience, turn these off, turn on Maguscule Mode, turn off Reverse Interlinear, turn off the English sublinear text, and set the word padding slider to zero: Now you have an ancient manuscript simulator! And then click "Reset Display Settings" because no one reads like that anymore...
  • New line after each verse: for those who prefer this format.
  • Reverse Interlinear: When checked, it uses the GHT English-ized word order. When unchecked, it displays my best reconstruction of the original Greek word order. (Many of the most common manuscript variations are in untranslatable word order and I did not put a significant amount of effort into selecting the correct one during the back-translation process.)
  • Highlight Search Results: When checked, any words that match existing search terms in the search box will be highlighted. Note that this does not distinguish between a valid result and an invalid result for multi-word constrained searches.
  • Format English: When checked, the English text will be formatted with my personal preference for pleasant display, reducing the clutter from brackets by means of smaller, off-color text and using less intrustive half-brackets instead of curly braces.

There are two word properties that are not available to be shown on screen. They are marked with "(in pop-up)". By default, they do not appear in the pop-up, but are available if desired:

  • Show Alternates: Shows a list of different ways the GHT translates this exact inflection. Warning: there will be some noticeable performance impact by selecting this option.
  • Transliteration: Shows a very rough transliteration of the Greek word. Note, this is a basic crutch for those who are new to the Greek alphabet and is not meant to be a rigorous transliteration. There are pronunciation nuances such as rough breathing which are not accounted for. Consider that the most basic step in learning Greek is to learn the alpha-bet[a]. It is twenty-four letters and many of them are similar to their Latin counterparts.

Max Results: Sets how many verses or entries to display at a time when making a large search. This value also limits the number of verses to display when selecting by reference.

Font size, word padding, word borders, and type-face selection boxes are all straightforward; play with them to find your preferred viewing experience.

Reset Display Settings: Puts you back in the default, Ghukek's preferred viewing experience.

Searching:

To search, type text into the search bar and click 'Search'. You may also click on any clickable string in the body of the text or in the popups to automatically search that string. Use the 'Greek Keyboard' if you do not have a Greek keyboard set up in your operating system and want to type in Greek. When 'Greek Keyboard' is checked, the search bar will automatically convert your input to Greek characters to allow you to search for Greek words. Click the '?' button to see an image of a Greek keyboard if you don't know how to type in Greek. You may search for multiple words at a time.

The settings in the 'Search' popup allow you to customize your search parameters. The explanation for these are as follows:

  • Exact Match: When checked, the search will only show words that are exactly as what you entered (case insensitive). Otherwise, it will return all partial matches. (Warning, you may need 'Normalize English' to be checked to get the results you expect. See below.)
  • Center Ref: When checked, this will center the verse containing the search terms in its context. Otherwise, the verse containing the search terms will be shown as the start of its context. For example, with a context of 5 verses, "the jesus tears." will show John 11:35-39 when unchecked or John 11:33-37 when checked.
  • Show Context: When checked, this will return search results in the verse they appear in plus as much surrounding context as the user selects using 'Show __ verses'. Otherwise it will just return a list of search results and the verse reference they appear in. (Note that any multi-word searches will always show in context.)
  • Unique Words: When checked, this will only show uniqe word pairs rather than every result. This is useful if a user is trying to look at all the different ways a specific word may be translated or inflected. (Note that 'Show Context' takes priority over 'Unique Words'.)
  • De-punctuate: When checked, this will ignore punctuation and pull text out of nested brackets. For example, a search for "of{Jesus}" will not show cases of "Jesus}" (from "of{the Jesus}") unless this is checked.
  • Ordered: When searching for multiple words, this forces the words to appear in the order they were searched. So, "Jesus Anointed" will not return verses that have "Anointed Jesus" (e.g. Acts 5:42). Note that this setting will work for whichever word order you have currently checked. Thus, "ου μη" (Exact Match, Ordered, Adjacent) will return a lot of results in interlinear order, but zero in reverse interlinear.
  • Adjacent: When searching for multiple words, this forces the words to be adjacent to each other. So, "Jesus Anointed" will not return "Jesus, the being-said 'Anointed'" (e.g. Matthew 1:18).
  • Expand Morph: Due to my innovation to use an expanded set of morphology letters to account for inflections with multiple grammatical options, this option allows the user to capture all letter options for a specific search. For example, searching for "A" for "accusative" should return anything marked with "B" for "accusative/nominative". When checked, it will search this way. When unchecked, it will only search for exact letter matches.

For searching, the following information will be useful:

  • A search "word" is any individual word unit. A word consists of propertes such as the original Greek word, its corresponding English translation, the morphology/parsing/grammar data, the Strong's concordance number, and my personal etymological categorization called "roots".
  • A search "term" is any individual property of a word. You can search for any property.
  • You can combine search terms. A space-separated search ("[term1] [term2]") will look for multiple words at a time. A symbol-separated search ("[term1]+[term2]" or "[term1]|[term2]") will combine the search terms and search for one word according to both terms. You can combine space-separated searches and symbol-separated searches. You may use as many terms as you want.
  • For multiple-word searches, with everything unchecked, the search will check the entire selected context for the words, no matter how far apart, out of order, or partial matching they may be. To restrict your search, you would want to reduce the 'Verse Range', check 'Exact Match', 'Ordered', or 'Adjacent' and any combination of these.
  • To combine multiple terms in one word, use the + symbol to request that both search terms be applied. For example "Jesus+N-AMS" will only get cases where Jesus is the object of a verb. You can also use the | symbol to request either case, for example "Jesus|Anointed" will get all cases of Jesus or Anointed. This also works when combined with a space separated multi-word search.
  • When searching by morphology tag, you can use the underscore (_) character to create wildcards. For example "Adj-A_" will return all accusative adjectives without regard for gender or number. "V-_O_-_" will likewise return all optative verbs.
  • To search within my roots data, prefix a period '.' to the term.
  • To enforce "exact match" on only one term while allowing other terms to be partial matches, prefix an "=" to the term.
  • To negate a term, (i.e. return all results that do not include the term), prefix a '~' to the term.

The information listed above is a bit technical. I encourage you to use my "Build Query" tool to assist you. Experiment with it. This search function is extremely powerful.

Panels:

Use the settings in the "Panels" popup to enable a second panel. By default, the second panel will work exactly like the first panel. All of your display and search settings are panel-specific. That is, you can have English showing on one, and Greek on the other. Clicking to search will send the search results to the active panel, not necessarily the panel you are clicking on. You can activate a panel by clicking any blank space (usually toward the end of a line or near a verse reference marker).

"Taller Panels" will make it so that the panels can nearly fill the screen. By default, the page will be entirely visible on your browser window. Enabling "taller panels" allows you to scroll down to hide UI. This is useful for viewing on smaller screens.

"Parallel Reference" links the two panels together such that a reference (Book/Chapter/Verse) call will load in both panels simultaneously. Useful for Alternate Translation mode explained below or using side-by-side rather than interlinear English/Greek since each panel can have its own display settings. Note: When only this is active, searches are still sent only to the active panel.

"Parallel Search" operates with the same principle as parallel reference. However, it does not search both panels with the same term. Rather, when a search finds a list of verses to display, the same verses will be shown in the alternate panel. This can be useful for comparing how different translations translate a given word or phrase. Since this only works for verse-based search results, single-word search results will still only be sent to the active panel.

"Scroll Link" links the scrolling of the two panels together.

"Swap Panels" will take the content and settings of each panel and swap their places.

Alternate Translations:

Found in the "Panels" popup. These only show up in the second panel, thus "Swap Panels" is disabled when an alternate translation is selected.

The GHT team is not responsible for the content of other translations, and their inclusion in this tool should not be considered endorsement. Any errors, omissions, additions, or interpretations remain the responsibility of the translation source organization.

Alternate translations are provided as a convenience and in the awareness that the user will want to compare. The reader is cautioned to be careful not to rely too heavily on the alternate translations, given their tendency for "overly loose and interpretive translating and paraphrasing, as well as with the traditions of the status quo and corresponding lack of due diligence to the original text".

Alternate translation selections are not included in the overall persistent-state mechanism of this tool. This is not a bug, but a deliberate design choice given the intent of the tool as a GHT service.

"VS" translations: These provide in-line difference information between two translations which are identical save for a textual basis shift. See here

for a more thorough explanation.

See here for a list of sources.

Sharing:

The tool can save the current reference selection to the URL so that the user can share a passage via link. Or, the user can share a particular search result. See the 'URL Save' buttons.

Alternatively, since the OS-level select/copy functionality is broken by the html elements needed for interlinear display; to copy on-screen text, use the 'Copy Text' buttons to copy all Greek or English text to your clipboard when you are verse-display mode.

The table copy button will copy a word list in a comma separated value format.

All buttons in this category will be based on the currently active panel.

Navigation:

The back and forward buttons at the top left of the page bring you to your last render state. It stores up to 100 renders in history.

The navigation buttons at the bottom of the page are relatively self-explanatory. They bring you forward or back by one chapter, page, or verse. A page is defined as the number of verses currently rendered.

You can also use navigation arrow keys to navigate book, chapter, page, and verse. Use the left /right arrow keys for the verse, and the up/down arrow keys for the page. Shift + left/right moves the chapter, and ctrl + left/right moves the book.

When searching, an additional page navigation button may appear, showing that you have more search results than the current maximum per-page. You can use the buttons or the left/right or the up/down arrow keys.

Important Translator Notes

The following is small selection from Garth's introduction. For more information, click on "GHT Source" and click on "Introduction (Please read!)..."

Notation, punctuation, capitalization

Every word, or construction between spaces, including possible hyphens and slash characters, or as demarcated within underscore characters, maps to one, single, corresponding word in the original Greek text, unless it is in square brackets. I separately translate every single word in the Greek, something that no other translation does. I use

  • square brackets to denote something I have added for clarity that is not in the original text.
  • An [ing] on a participle means it is an aorist or future participle, not a present participle.
  • As noted in more detail below, I use
    • curly brackets to denote dative and genitive cases and
    • a colon to denote third-person imperatives.
  • I liberally use
    • hyphens to bring out etymological/morphemes, compound words, and single words from the original that do not have a single English correspondence but can be expressed using multiple English words and/or English morphemes, and
    • underscore to insert separate original words into a hyphenated sequence (usually "_not_").
  • I use the slash character where I need to convey that a word could be either one or the other English word, or a sense of both or something in between.

Since interrogatives are not punctuated in the Greek, and are not even explicit, I let the text flow as in the original and insert question mark characters in square brackets. Beyond that, punctuation is simply a best-effort attempt to follow English convention. There is little to no punctuation in the original Greek text, and not in the English sense or English convention. I capitalize proper names as in English, but there is no capitalization scheme in Greek. Verse number placement adheres to the convention originated by the Geneva Bible.

Important points in lexicality and grammar, issues

I use "of{}" and "to{}" for genitive and dative cases, respectively, but everyone should keep in mind that these are not prepositions, nor do they, without actual prepositions, create prepositional phrases in the original Greek. The genitive case simply points from an object and the dative case to an object. However, when I create an English prepositional phrase from it, I don't always keep prefixing every consecutive genitive or dative word accordingly. Instead, I enclose multiple separate words in curly brackets, which are all genitive or dative, as the case may be.

The Greek language has both second and third person imperative verbs, whereas English only has second person imperatives. To translate the third person, I construct the phrase using a colon. For example, Matt 5:16, "the light of you: shine," such that it is the light that is being given the imperative, the command, not the person being addressed. This eliminates the traditional use of "let" (e.g. "let your light shine"), where "let" is a verb that only means "allow," still in the second person, and does not bring out the imperative sense of the actual verb (i.e. "allow your light to shine" has "allow" as an imperative in the second person and "shine" as an infinitive).
